meta.title: We’re going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything
meta.author: frontsideair

comments.author: agwa
comments.text: Worth noting that the AWS limits only work if you use the new signup "experience". This "experience" comes with a number of limitations, including, surprisingly, the inability to use multiple regions. If you want to remove the limitations, you have to enable "advanced features", which makes the spend limits go away

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
Ouch! I saw it was limited but I didn't realize how limited.

(Amusingly enough I only learned the feature existed when I ran my proof reading prompt against the first draft with Claude and it fact checked my claim that AWS didn't have the feature.)

comments.author: zem
comments.text: I'm many ways I consider I myself incredibly lucky that my source of income is a 9-5 job and everything else I do is purely for personal enjoyment and I don't need to ever think about monetising it. that lets me simply nope out of a lot of adversarial relationships with tech companies. aws pulling dark patterns like this? fine, never touching aws, I have no customer base to consider scaling issues for. google arbitrarily banning app engine users? can't risk my gmail account, never touching their paas stuff. apple requires app store approval for everything? never writing an ios app. it's a very liberating way to interact with tech and I genuinely feel bad for the people who have to deal with these services because that's where the money is.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
Why is it that surprising? They have throughput-optimised eventual consistency, with pretty significant global convergence delays (apparently at some point they did the same with warehouse inventory data…). So making limits across regions work is significantly harder.

I would not be surprised if decision flow was «we need hard limits for small users (or regulation forces the limits for everyone)» → «we need to define small users as single-region» → «how do we market the new account option»

comments.author: Gaelan
comments.text: I mean, there’s a straightforward option: make a best effort to kill everything reasonably soon after the limit is breached, bill the customer no more than the limit, and eat the occasional losses. This should be fine as long as you have some reasonable mechanism to stop someone from creating loads of accounts, which I assume they already have for free tier reasons?

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text: They probably do not want this to be an option for large enterprise deployments because it might stop the slippery-slope development patterns. If people need to go to finance to authorise raising the cap every month, someone might actually notice that AWS dependency is bad, actualyl.

comments.author: Student
comments.text: They could just allow limits per region

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text: I guess marketing didn't want to draw too much attention to them not being able to do things across regions?

comments.author: hyperpape
comments.text: I can’t quite tell if you’re defending the implementation here, but that does seem like marketing’s problem.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text: My honest opinion is: AWS is approximately never a good choice in any case, and there are always multiple reasons it is not surprising that they do things badly.

comments.author: tclancy
comments.text: It’s not the least bit surprising once you accept AWS ux is actively hostile. But in a normal world, not everyone who needs support in multiple regions needs world-class consistency. Some times they just have to check two boxes and it does not feel wild the more likely case for multi regions needs users would be “I don’t want to authorize a runaway bill either”. What, exactly, are you defending?

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
I do in fact think that expecting AWS to be actively hostile and bad fit for approximately any usecase at all is the correct approach. Also, expecting Amazon to be actively hostile if they can get away with that is a good bet.

The shape of my argument is «why is it surprising, they always refuse to do this right» — I am not defending Amazon's choices, I am arguing for never expecting Amazon to do things right anywhere near specific topics.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
I think soft caps on AWS were not just insufficient, they also plain didn't work: many of the horror stories included the first notification when the bill was already way past the configured limit. I guess this became enough of a regulatory risk to introduce hard caps and eat the difference when their billing system cannot stay close to realtime.

But also, assuming LLMs can do standard well-known things, there is a solution with hard budget cap by default and inavoidably. Install stuff on VPSes with purely monthly pricing, do not give agent access to order more (so no hoster management UI access, just SSH access to VPS). There are clauses in ToS about things that get your VPS shut down, and in some cases your account terminated (like on AWS, of course), but what you pay is known in advance.

comments.author: landon
comments.text:
I expect that most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill.


These businesses have no say in the matter, they are serfs. Why on earth would a business that stands to collect on these massive mistakes put up guardrails against them? That's leaving money on the table.

If somebody tripped and dropped $10k on your patio you'd probably give it back, you're also not a product designer for a cloud host, and this is why. Think like a ravenous greedy ghoul with an unending thirst for money and no integrity or decency, and you'll start to understand how these "experiences" are designed.

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
Plenty of these businesses do offer a hard budget limit now, so they clearly see value in not losing a potentially long-lasting commercial relationship with a customer over a one-time mistake.

It's also common for surprise overages to result in a customer support case that eventually ends up with the customer being refunded.

comments.author: landon
comments.text: The fact that this isn't the default everywhere is wild to me. "Bankrupt my company in service of itself" seems like behavior nobody would opt in to if if was opt-in.

comments.author: andersmurphy
comments.text:
Wonder if this makes VPS and dedicated servers more popular. You can scale so far on a single machine these days. Kinda makes things much simpler.

I guess the other option is just to write code by hand.

comments.author: jcd
comments.text: Return an error like a 429? Seems sensible enough. Alternatively software businesses may actually have to have workable unit economics. It will be interesting to see what happens as software if software becomes a commodity market. Maybe margins will shrink.
